A pleat is a deliberately made fold in a piece of fabric, where the fabric is doubled over onto itself and then held in place at one point — usually stitched down at the top — while the rest of the fold is left free and open.

Think of it this way: take a piece of paper, pinch a section of it, fold it over, and press it flat. That folded section is the pleat. In real clothing, this is done with fabric instead of paper.

A pleat looks like a neat, structured crease or tuck in fabric. At the point where it is stitched down, the fabric lies flat and controlled. Below that point, the extra fold of fabric opens up loosely, allowing the garment to flare out, breathe, or move.

If you've ever seen formal trousers (dress pants), look at the front near the waistband — you'll likely see one or two vertical folds running downward. Those are pleats.

Pleats serve two main purposes: function and appearance.

Functionally, a pleat adds extra fabric to a garment in a controlled way. This extra fabric gives the wearer more room to move. Without pleats, trousers would be tight and stiff when you walk, sit, or climb stairs. The pleat quietly holds spare fabric in reserve. When you move, it opens up to give you the space you need.

Aesthetically, pleats give a garment a clean, structured, tailored look. They signal formality and craftsmanship. A pleated skirt has a graceful, full silhouette. Pleated trousers look crisp and intentional rather than casual or fitted.

Pleats appear most commonly in clothing:

  • Trousers / dress pants — pleats near the waistband at the front give room around the hips and thighs.
  • Skirts — pleated skirts use multiple pleats around the waist to create fullness and volume in the lower part of the skirt.
  • Kilts — the back of a traditional kilt is densely pleated.
  • Dresses and blouses — pleats may appear at the chest, shoulders, or waist for both movement and shape.
  • Curtains — pleated curtains have folds at the top (where they hang from a rod) that make them hang beautifully and give them a full, rich look.
  • Pillowcases and bed linen — decorative pleats are sometimes added for an elegant finish.

Beyond fabric, you might also hear "pleat" used loosely to describe a similar fold structure in paper or other flexible materials, though clothing is by far its most common home.

Although they all share the same basic idea — a fold in fabric — pleats come in a few different forms, depending on which direction the folds go:

Knife pleat — All the folds go in the same direction, like a series of steps all facing the same way. When you look at a pleated skirt that fans out as the wearer twirls, knife pleats are usually responsible.

Box pleat — Two folds are made to face away from each other on the front surface of the fabric, meeting at a central point on the back. This creates a flat, box-like panel on the front with a wide hidden fold on the back. Box pleats are common in school uniform skirts and formal shirts.

Inverted box pleat — The opposite of a box pleat. Two folds face toward each other on the front, meeting at a central seam. The extra fabric is hidden on the front and fans outward at the back. You'll see this on the back panels of blazers and jackets, allowing the fabric to open slightly when the wearer moves.

Accordion pleat — A series of sharp, alternating folds that go back and forth like the bellows of an accordion instrument. These are closely spaced and create a very full, rippling effect when the garment moves.

Kick pleat — A single, short pleat placed at the hem (the bottom edge) of a narrow skirt. Its only job is functional: it gives just enough room for the wearer to take a normal stride without tearing or straining the skirt.
How a pleat differs from similar things

It helps to distinguish a pleat from a few related terms:

  • A dart is a stitched fold that is sewn completely shut — it tapers to a point and is used to shape the garment to the body's curves. A dart does not open up; it is entirely closed. A pleat, by contrast, is only held at one end and remains open and functional along its length.
  • A gather is when fabric is bunched or ruffled by pulling a thread through it, creating a soft, irregular, casual fullness. Gathers are loose and unpredictable in their folds. Pleats are deliberate, sharp, and precise.
  • A tuck is a stitched fold, similar to a pleat but usually sewn down entirely along its length for decorative effect rather than for adding functional volume. Tucks are typically smaller and are purely aesthetic.
A simple mental image to remember it

Imagine you are folding a map or a paper fan. Each time you fold one section of paper over the previous one, you are making something very much like a pleat. In fabric, that same idea is used — but only part of the fold is stitched down, so the rest can open up and move freely.

That combination — structure at one end, freedom at the other — is what makes a pleat both useful and elegant.
